paragraphs: This checklist is for self-reflection only. It is not a hiring standard, ability score, or assessment of job competence. This page covers U.S. O*NET / SOC 11-1021.00, General and Operations Managers (the fixed index uses the same occupational name in Chinese; common industry titles include business manager, center manager, department manager, district manager, general manager (GM), operations director, operations general manager, operations manager, plant superintendent, and store manager). The official scope is to plan, direct, or coordinate the operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations. Duties include formulating policies, managing daily operations, and planning the use of materials and human resources, but are too diverse and general to be classified under a single management or administrative function such as personnel, purchasing, or administrative services. Management is usually exercised through subordinate supervisors; first-line supervisors are excluded. Core work includes reviewing financial statements, sales or activity reports, and other performance data to measure productivity or goal achievement and identify areas needing cost reduction or improvement; directing and coordinating business or departmental activities involving production, pricing, sales, or distribution; directing administrative activities directly related to providing products and services; preparing staff schedules and assigning specific duties; directing or coordinating financial or budget activities to fund operations, maximize investments, or increase efficiency; planning or directing activities requiring coordination with other department managers, such as promotions; performing personnel functions such as selection, training, and evaluation; developing departmental policies, goals, and procedures with board members, organizational heads, or staff; overseeing suppliers to ensure that required materials or services are provided effectively within budget; managing the flow of materials into and out of production facilities to ensure operational efficiency and sustainability; setting prices or credit terms for materials or services based on customer-demand forecasts; performing floor work such as greeting and assisting customers, stocking, or taking inventory; developing or implementing product marketing strategies, including advertising campaigns and promotions; directing non-sales departments such as advertising or purchasing; implementing or overseeing environmental management or sustainability programs such as recycling, energy conservation, and waste management; planning store layouts or designing displays; and recommending new facility locations or overseeing remodeling and renovation of existing facilities. The work involves frequent decisions, intensive communication, substantial responsibility for others' safety and outcomes, and typical workweeks often exceeding 40 hours. O*NET's 2024 major-industry context shows professional, scientific, and technical services at 12% and retail trade at 12%; 76% is the remainder for other industries calculated from the displayed rounded integers, with no internal breakdown provided.

Practice brief | G1 synthetic case | Two service sites, A / B, have after-sales service and dispatch coordinated by two subordinate supervisors. There are 100 confirmed orders for next week (A60, B40); this week, 90 orders were completed at a cost of 9,000 yuan. Regular capacity is A50 orders and B40 orders; approved fixed costs of 8,000 yuan cover 90 orders. An additional 10 orders of outsourced capacity can be purchased at 120 yuan per order, adding 1,200 yuan in spending. Targets: complete 100 orders, achieve an on-time delivery rate of at least 95%, and keep costs at or below 10,000 yuan; standard working hours and safety checks must not be reduced. Simulated authority: you may add no more than 1,000 yuan in spending within the established plan; higher amounts require written approval from a superior. Outsourcing suppliers require purchasing / quality review. Do not independently change staffing arrangements or safety checks, or promise unapproved orders. Use identifiers only, with no personal information. Within 90 minutes, complete a metrics / definitions table, resource allocation, cost calculation, and approval / escalation log; state how many orders can be promised before approval. All data are assumptions for a paper exercise and must not be used for actual purchasing or staffing.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 11-1021.00 work-context data show: frequency of decision making, 93% report daily; freedom to make decisions, 86% report a lot of freedom; determining tasks and priorities, 73% report a lot of freedom; email, 88% daily; telephone, 88% daily; face-to-face discussions, 86% daily; constant contact with others, 76%; working in a team, 79% report extremely important; coordinating or leading others, 57% report extremely important; responsibility for others' health and safety, 61% report very high responsibility; impact on coworkers' or company results, 72% report very important results; dealing with external customers or the public, 61% report extremely important; typical workweek, 70% report more than 40 hours; environmentally controlled indoor work, 80% daily. If you can first clarify goals and authority when information is incomplete, assign responsibilities and track metrics, and are willing to handle conflict and exceptions and document outcomes, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also reports for 11-1021.00: typical workweek, 70% report more than 40 hours; time pressure, 41% report daily; dealing with unpleasant people, 59% report once a month or more but not every week; conflict situations, 35% report once a month or more but not every week; level of competition, 32% report highly competitive. This occupation addresses cross-functional goals, resources, people, customer commitments, and risk events. A single unauthorized contract or expenditure, weakening of safety controls to increase output, distorted metric definition, or overloaded schedule can cause accidents, service disruption, compliance consequences, and staff turnover. The 61% reporting very high responsibility for others' health and safety means that your decisions directly affect other people's working conditions. If you struggle to make explicit tradeoffs between conflicting goals, accept responsibility for others' safety and outcomes, or maintain documentation and escalation under sustained overtime and exception pressure, treat these as practical costs requiring serious consideration.

Judging the responsibility | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same operational task: translate goals into operations (convert strategic goals into trackable metrics and resource plans, arrange staffing and shifts, and monitor costs, quality, delivery, and customer outcomes); manage authority and controls (exercise powers within the articles of association and delegated authority, obtain and document process-based approval for major contracts, spending, pricing, staffing, and safety-control changes, and never bypass controls); and accept defined job responsibilities (be accountable for operating results, team safety, and customer commitments, and report to superiors or the board under the organization's governance structure). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as producing operational metrics, staffing schedules, and resource plans for a fictional organization; a cost-reduction or improvement proposal with an explanation of tradeoffs; or an operational review and risk register, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire's conclusion.

Direct answer | General and operations managers on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 11-1021.00. Their work falls into several categories: (one) Goals and performance management: review financial statements, sales or activity reports, and other performance data to measure productivity or goal achievement and identify areas needing cost reduction or improvement. (two) Operational direction and coordination: direct and coordinate business or departmental activities involving production, pricing, sales, or distribution; direct administrative activities directly related to providing products and services; plan or direct activities requiring coordination with other department managers; and manage the flow of materials into and out of production facilities. (three) People and organization: prepare staff schedules and assign specific duties; perform personnel functions such as selection, training, and evaluation; and develop departmental policies, goals, and procedures with board members, organizational heads, or staff. (four) Financial and commercial decisions: direct or coordinate financial or budget activities to support operating funds, investments, and efficiency; set prices or credit terms for materials or services based on customer-demand forecasts; and develop or implement product marketing strategies. (five) Supply chain and facilities: oversee suppliers to ensure effective provision of required materials or services within budget; plan store layouts or design displays; recommend new facility locations or oversee remodeling and renovation of existing facilities; and implement or oversee environmental management or sustainability programs. Four or more categories connect in a cycle: read performance data → translate goals into metrics and resource plans → arrange people and work → direct and coordinate cross-department execution → monitor costs, quality, delivery, and customer outcomes → handle exceptions and report to superiors or the board. This page distinguishes this occupation from adjacent administrative services managers, purchasing managers, sales managers, financial managers, industrial production managers, and first-line supervisors. A managerial title does not confer the governance powers of the board or top management.

O*NET and BLS occupational-profile highlights | This page covers U.S. SOC 11-1021.00, General and Operations Managers, a management occupation labeled Bright Outlook by O*NET and updated in 2026. Its official scope is to plan, direct, or coordinate operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations. Duties include formulating policies, managing daily operations, and planning the use of materials and human resources, but are too diverse and general to be classified under a single management or administrative function. Management is usually exercised through subordinate supervisors; first-line supervisors are excluded. O*NET lists 17 tasks, including 9 core tasks: reviewing performance data, 80; coordinating business activities, 79; administrative activities, 75; scheduling, 75; financial budgeting, 73; collaborative activities, 71; personnel, 70; policies and goals, 69; and supplier oversight, 61. The 8 supplemental tasks are materials flow, 76; pricing and credit, 75; floor work, 72; marketing, 64; non-sales departments, 63; sustainability, 53; layout, 48; and facility location and remodeling, 45. Supplemental does not mean a core duty for everyone. The highest-importance work activities are working with computers (87) and getting information (86), followed by communicating with supervisors, peers, and subordinates (84); making decisions and solving problems (83); establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships (82); identifying objects, actions, and events (81); guiding, directing, and motivating subordinates (80); organizing, planning, and prioritizing work (80); judging the qualities of objects and services (78); and processing information (77).

Obtain approval under governance procedures for contracts, spending, pricing, staffing, safety-control changes, or matters beyond delegated authority. Governance and data boundaries | In mainland China, a company manager under Article 74 of the Company Law performs duties under the articles of association or board authorization, and senior managers owe duties of loyalty and diligence under Article 180. This does not automatically cover every title of operations manager, plant manager, or store manager. A company meeting Article 75 may have a single director exercise board powers. Organizations should define each professional role's approval, review, and sign-off scope; it cannot be inferred from a managerial title. For personal information identifying employees or customers, check the lawful basis, purpose, necessary scope, notification, and applicable exceptions under the Personal Information Protection Law. Manage general business data under organizational permissions and confidentiality rules; not all commercial data are personal information. Check safety inspections and controls against job risks, regulations, and organizational procedures.

Records and collaboration | Follow organizational procedures to record operational metrics and definitions; resource and budget decisions and their basis; schedules and staffing arrangements; suppliers, contracts, delivery, and acceptance; exceptions, responses, responsible people, and deadlines; and reports to superiors or the board. Immediately report distorted metrics, unauthorized commitments, bypassed controls, or safety and compliance risks within delegated authority and address them through established procedures. Do not backdate or fabricate records. Genuine corrections must preserve the original record and state the time, basis, and reviewer.

Boundary conclusion | This page covers U.S. SOC 11-1021.00. The main distinction from adjacent roles lies in the object of the work and level of delegated authority. This occupation addresses daily operations across multiple departments or locations, producing verifiable operational metrics, resource plans, performance reviews, cross-department decisions, and escalation records. Administrative services managers (11-3012.00) address support functions such as administration, facilities, and records; purchasing managers (11-3061.00) address purchasing, suppliers, and contract execution; sales managers (11-2022.00) address sales targets, sales teams, and customer relationships; financial managers (11-3031.00) address financial planning, reporting, funds, and risk control; industrial production managers (11-3051.00) address production plans, manufacturing processes, capacity, quality, and safety. First-line supervisors are explicitly excluded from this occupation's official scope. Work objects and levels of delegated authority differ, so powers over budgets, contracts, pricing, staffing, and safety-control changes cannot be carried across roles. A managerial title does not automatically include governance powers belonging to the board or top management.

Core principles of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group and adjacent roles aim to translate goals into measurable operating results within delegated authority and accept responsibility for resources, people, and risks. They differ in their work objects and functional scope: some address cross-department daily operations, others administrative and facilities support, purchasing and suppliers, sales and customers, finance and funds, or production and manufacturing processes.

This occupation's core purpose | Address daily operations across multiple departments or locations and translate organizational goals into measurable operating results within the articles of association, delegated authority, and governance structure: read performance data; translate goals into metrics, resource plans, and staffing plans; direct and coordinate cross-department execution; monitor costs, quality, delivery, and customer outcomes; handle exceptions and define responsibilities and deadlines; and escalate within delegated authority or report to the board and superiors. This makes operational processes, results, and decision rationales traceable and consistent with governance, safety, and compliance requirements.

Main objects and basis of adjacent roles | Administrative services managers work from administrative, facilities, records, and purchasing-support functions and organizational rules; purchasing managers from purchasing needs, suppliers, contracts, and budgets; sales managers from sales targets, sales teams, customer relationships, and market strategies; financial managers from financial planning, reporting, funds, risk control, and accounting standards; and industrial production managers from production plans, manufacturing processes, capacity, quality, and safety procedures.

Main objects and basis of this occupation | The work addresses cross-functional operational goals, operational metrics, and performance data; budgets, costs, capacity, and resources; personnel, schedules, duties, and evaluations; customer commitments and service standards; suppliers, contracts, materials, and facilities; and processes, control systems, and risk events. Its basis is the company's articles of association, board resolutions, delegated authority, job descriptions, and organizational rules, together with governance, safety, quality, compliance, and data-protection requirements.

General and operations managers oversee operations across multiple departments or locations, usually organizing people, resources, and daily execution through subordinate supervisors and delivering operational metrics, resource plans, and review records. The U.S. definition excludes first-line supervisors. Insufficient evidence: this page has not obtained a wage distribution for the precise occupation in China.

Core processes of adjacent roles | Administrative services managers focus on organizing, implementing, and improving support functions such as administration, facilities, records, and purchasing; purchasing managers on the process from purchasing needs through supplier selection, contract execution, delivery, and acceptance; sales managers on breaking down sales targets, managing teams, and maintaining customer relationships and channels; financial managers on budgets, forecasts, accounting, reporting, funds, and risk control; and industrial production managers on issuing production plans, controlling manufacturing processes, capacity, quality, and safety.

Core process of this occupation | Read performance data and align organizational goals; translate goals into operational metrics, resource plans, and staffing plans; direct and coordinate cross-department execution; monitor costs, quality, delivery, and customer outcomes; handle exceptions and designate responsible people and deadlines; and escalate within delegated authority or report to the board and superiors. Each step must be documented under organizational rules and delegated authority and be reviewable by superiors, the board, or internal audit.

Main outputs of adjacent roles | Administrative services managers produce administrative and facilities service standards, implementation records, and improvement proposals; purchasing managers produce purchasing contracts, supplier evaluations, delivery and acceptance records, and cost-saving records; sales managers produce sales plans, sales results, and customer and channel records; financial managers produce budgets, financial reports, and conclusions on funds and risk controls; and industrial production managers produce production plans and output, quality, safety, and equipment records.

Main outputs of this occupation | Verifiable operational metrics and definitions; resource, budget, staffing, and shift plans; cross-department decisions and authorization records; performance reviews and improvement proposals; reports on costs, quality, delivery, and customer outcomes; supplier, contract, delivery, and acceptance records; records of risks, exceptions, responses, responsible people, and deadlines; and reports and escalation records submitted to superiors or the board.

Responsibility in adjacent roles | Responsibilities in the same group and adjacent roles are usually defined by the employing organization, delegated authority, rules, and professional procedures, and generally concern the organization, customers, employees, product quality, delivery, and compliance.

Responsibility in this occupation | This occupation is accountable for operating results, resources, staffing arrangements, customer commitments, and team safety within delegated authority, and for metrics, decisions, records, and reports completed under organizational rules. The board or superiors and relevant professional leads decide through established procedures on contracts, spending, pricing, staffing, and safety-control changes beyond delegated authority; major contracts and investments; and governance, compliance, and disciplinary matters. This occupation does not replace their decisions.

Authority and approval in adjacent roles | Authority in the same group and adjacent roles comes from organizational delegation, rules, and professional procedures. It generally does not include independently deciding on contracts, spending, staffing, or safety-control changes beyond the role's functions. Cross-functional matters and those exceeding thresholds should be referred to superiors or the relevant governance and professional roles.

Authority and approval in this occupation | Directing operations, arranging personnel, assigning duties, and overseeing suppliers must remain within the company's articles of association, delegation from the board or superiors, and organizational rules. Contracts, spending, pricing, staffing, safety-control changes, major purchasing and investments, and compliance or disciplinary matters require approval through governance procedures or referral to the board and relevant professional leads. Do not make unauthorized commitments or bypass controls.

Limits on conclusions in adjacent roles | Conclusions in the same group and adjacent roles are generally limited to the function, department, and individual's responsibilities, and usually do not constitute a final determination of the organization's overall operating performance or governance compliance. Conclusions across functions or organizations, or involving governance, have limits on their applicability.

Limits on conclusions in this occupation | Operational conclusions must state only verifiable facts about metrics, resources, and decisions and distinguish measured, estimated, and forecast values. Do not make unapproved commitments on matters beyond delegated authority, such as contracts, spending, staffing, safety-control changes, or investments. Distorted metrics, unauthorized commitments, bypassed controls, and major safety or compliance risks must be escalated or referred. Metric definitions must also withstand review by superiors, the board, internal audit, and regulators.

Checks before joining | Use the following six items one by one before applying or joining to avoid inferring actual duties and authority from a job title or promotional wording. Base findings on written recruitment information, the employment contract, job description, company articles of association, authorization documents, and organizational rules, and continue confirming them after joining. This page lists directions for checking only; it is not any organization's formal requirements checklist. Special note: authority varies greatly in this occupation. Confirm the role's actual functional scope across operations, production, sales, purchasing, and administration; span of control and reporting relationships; and authorization thresholds for contracts, spending, staffing, and safety-control changes.

Checking guidance | Similar titles can involve very different duties and authority. Some roles are accountable for cross-department operations and profit and loss, some focus on a single function such as administration, purchasing, sales, finance, or production, some on stores or multiple sites, and some on projects or regions. Authorization thresholds and reporting relationships for contracts, spending, pricing, staffing, and safety-control changes also differ between organizations.

01 Actual duties and authority boundaries | Check whether the role truly carries cross-department responsibility for operations, outcomes, and resource decisions or mainly involves execution or coordination within one function. Check the span of control, subordinate teams, reporting relationships, authorization thresholds and approval paths for contracts, spending, pricing, staffing, purchasing, and safety-control changes, and responsibilities for reporting and escalating matters beyond authority.

Checking guidance | O*NET61% of respondents report very high responsibility for others' health and safety; these are U.S. context data. For a role in China, separately check safety / governance training and authorization; duties of loyalty and diligence under the Company Law apply to the persons specified in that law.

02 Safety, compliance, and governance training | Ask the organization about safety, emergency response, conflicts of interest, internal controls, personal information, and confidentiality training applicable to this role's duties. Check the specific approval, review, sign-off, and exception-escalation authority of each professional role. Do not assume every person in charge has a statutory right to sign independently.

Checking guidance | U.S. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Four, considerable preparation. The zone's general description states that most occupations require a bachelor's degree and substantial experience and training; it is not a statistical finding that most respondents in this occupation require a bachelor's degree. An industry may require professional credentials or licensure, but a managerial title itself does not automatically confer professional sign-off or statutory authority.

03 Education, experience, and qualifications | Check whether a bachelor's degree or higher is required, commonly in business administration, business, management science, finance, or public administration, together with several or more years of relevant functional experience; whether functional certifications are required or preferred, such as Certified Manager Certification, Certified Facility Manager, APICS certification in planning and inventory management, or Certified Construction Manager; whether registered apprenticeships such as Operations Management and internal management-development programs are offered; and the internal conditions for obtaining sign-off and approval authority.

Checking guidance | For this occupation's typical workweek, 70% report more than 40 hours. Compensation often includes base annual salary, performance or year-end bonuses, long-term incentives, and allowances. Confirm working hours, performance definitions, incentive conditions, and assessment cycles in writing.

04 Pay, hours, and incentive basis | Check the proposed compensation components: base annual salary, performance or year-end bonuses, long-term or equity incentives, and role or location allowances. Check hours, on-call duties, travel arrangements, probation, assessment definitions, and how targets are set, as well as any agreements on responsibility for operating results, safety, and compliance and any accountability or recovery clauses.

Checking guidance | Interfaces with superiors, the board, finance, human resources, safety, quality, supply chain, customers, and suppliers define responsibility boundaries for operational decisions, commitments, and escalation and must be clarified beforehand.

05 Authority at interfaces with governance, professional functions, and external parties | Check reporting and approval authority and thresholds with superiors or the board; countersigning and consultation paths with finance, human resources, legal, safety, and quality roles; contract and delivery interfaces with purchasing and supply chain; authority for commitments and negotiations with customers and suppliers; and role arrangements for cross-department collaboration and exception handling.

Checking guidance | Traceability and documentation requirements for operational metrics, decisions, budgets, contracts, personnel, and safety records determine how operating, governance, compliance, and safety responsibilities are defined. Clarify rules for versions, amendments, archiving, permissions, and retention periods beforehand. Employee and customer information must also be managed under personal-information and business-information requirements.

06 Records, data, and documentation requirements | Check records of operational metrics, definitions, and data sources; budget and resource decisions and approvals; schedules, staffing arrangements, and evaluations; suppliers, contracts, delivery, and acceptance; safety, quality, compliance, incidents, and responses; and reports to superiors or the board, including version, amendment, archiving, retention, and access rules. Check duties to provide evidence and cooperate in operating, compliance, or safety disputes and regulatory inspections; requirements for authenticity of business and personnel data and the prohibition on backdating or fabrication; and requirements that genuine corrections preserve the original record and state the time, basis, and reviewer.

Introduction | The comparison below has four columns: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which choices it better suits. Operations, administration, sales, finance, production, and purchasing often connect within one organization, but connection does not mean interchangeability. Changing direction requires learning the new function's professional standards, compliance requirements, authority scope, and metric definitions.

Key difference: this occupation addresses daily operations across multiple departments or locations, breaks down goals, makes resource and staffing decisions, reviews performance, and accepts responsibility for operating results and team safety. Other roles focus respectively on administrative and facilities support, sales and customers, finance and funds, production and manufacturing processes, or purchasing and suppliers, and usually do not carry responsibility for the overall results of cross-functional operations.

Occupational definition | General and operations managers on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 11-1021.00, General and Operations Managers. The official scope is to plan, direct, or coordinate operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations. Duties include formulating policies, managing daily operations, and planning the use of materials and human resources, but are too diverse and general to be classified under a single management or administrative function. Management is usually exercised through subordinate supervisors; first-line supervisors are excluded. Tasks include both core and supplemental duties, with 9 / 8 read separately: review financial statements, sales or activity reports, and other performance data to measure productivity or goal achievement; direct and coordinate business or departmental activities involving production, pricing, sales, or distribution; direct administrative activities directly related to providing products and services; prepare staff schedules and assign specific duties; direct or coordinate financial or budget activities; plan or direct activities requiring coordination with other department managers; perform personnel functions such as selection, training, and evaluation; develop departmental policies, goals, and procedures with board members, organizational heads, or staff; oversee suppliers; manage materials flowing into and out of production facilities; set prices or credit terms based on customer-demand forecasts; perform floor work; develop or implement product marketing strategies; direct non-sales departments such as advertising or purchasing; implement or oversee environmental management and sustainability programs; plan store layouts or design displays; and recommend new facility locations or oversee remodeling and renovation. Outputs are operational metrics, resource and staffing plans, performance reviews, cross-department decisions, and escalation records. These are U.S. definitions; see this page's notes for mainland China's roles, statutory powers, and statistical definitions.

values: G1 synthetic case | Two service sites, A / B, have after-sales service and dispatch coordinated by two subordinate supervisors. An additional 10 orders of outsourced capacity can be purchased at 120 yuan per order, adding 1,200 yuan in spending. Targets: complete 100 orders, achieve an on-time delivery rate of at least 95%, and keep costs at or below 10,000 yuan. Standard working hours and safety checks must not be reduced. Simulated authority: you may add no more than 1,000 yuan in spending within the established plan; higher amounts require written approval from a superior. This week's unit cost is 9,000÷90=100 yuan. The proposed unit cost falls 8%, while total cost rises 200 yuan (approximately 2.22%); total cost does not fall.

The 1,200 yuan exceeds the simulated 1,000 yuan authority limit and requires superior approval and purchasing / quality review. Before approval, only 90 orders of regular capacity are available; do not promise 100 orders. A 95% on-time target means at least 95 orders completed on time; the actual on-time rate remains to be verified.

entries.answer: General and operations managers on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 11-1021.00: plan, direct, or coordinate operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations. Duties include formulating policies, managing daily operations, and planning the use of materials and human resources, but are too diverse and general to be classified under a single management or administrative function. Management is usually exercised through subordinate supervisors; first-line supervisors are excluded. Core work includes reviewing financial statements, sales or activity reports, and other performance data to measure productivity or goal achievement; directing and coordinating business or departmental activities involving production, pricing, sales, or distribution; preparing staff schedules and assigning specific duties; directing or coordinating financial or budget activities; overseeing suppliers and managing materials flowing into and out of production facilities; setting prices or credit terms based on customer-demand forecasts; performing personnel functions such as selection, training, and evaluation; developing departmental policies, goals, and procedures with board members, organizational heads, or staff; and handling exceptions and reporting to superiors or the board. Common employers include operations departments in manufacturing, retail, construction, professional services, and public services. This page uses U.S. occupational-classification definitions.

entries.answer: The key distinction lies in work objects and levels of delegated authority. This occupation addresses daily operations across multiple departments or locations and produces verifiable operational metrics, resource plans, performance reviews, cross-department decisions, and escalation records. Administrative services managers (11-3012.00) address support functions such as administration, facilities, and records; sales managers (11-2022.00) address sales targets, sales teams, and customer relationships; financial managers (11-3031.00) address financial planning, reporting, funds, and risk control; industrial production managers (11-3051.00) address production plans, manufacturing processes, capacity, quality, and safety; and purchasing managers (11-3061.00) address purchasing, suppliers, and contract execution. First-line supervisors are explicitly excluded from this occupation's official scope. Different work objects and authority levels mean that powers over budgets, contracts, pricing, staffing, and safety-control changes cannot be carried across roles.

subject.name: General and Operations Managers
subject.summary: General and operations managers correspond to U.S. O*NET / SOC 11-1021.00, General and Operations Managers: they plan, direct, or coordinate the operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations. Duties include formulating policies, managing daily operations, and planning the use of materials and human resources, but are too diverse and general to be classified under any single management or administrative function. They usually manage through subordinate supervisors; first-line supervisors are excluded. Core work includes reviewing financial statements, sales or activity reports, and other performance data to measure productivity or goal achievement; directing and coordinating business or departmental activities involving production, pricing, sales, or distribution; preparing staff schedules and assigning duties; directing or coordinating financial or budget activities; overseeing suppliers and managing the flow of materials into and out of production facilities; setting prices or credit terms based on demand forecasts; performing personnel functions such as selection, training, and evaluation; and developing departmental policies, goals, and procedures with board members, organizational heads, or staff. Official scope: Plan, direct, or coordinate the operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations.
